claim: In the early days of HIV treatment, drug resistance occurred rapidly and predictably in all patients.
source: In the early days of HIV treatment, drug resistance occurred rapidly and predictably in all patients, but under modern treatments, resistance arises slowly, if at all.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about historical HIV treatment outcomes.

claim: Under modern HIV treatments, resistance arises slowly, if at all.
source: In the early days of HIV treatment, drug resistance occurred rapidly and predictably in all patients, but under modern treatments, resistance arises slowly, if at all.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about modern HIV treatment outcomes.

claim: If many adaptive mutations arise simultaneously, then adaptation proceeds by soft selective sweeps in which multiple adaptive mutations spread concomitantly.
source: If many adaptive mutations arise simultaneously, then adaptation proceeds by soft selective sweeps in which multiple adaptive mutations spread concomitantly, but if adaptive mutations occur rarely in the population, then a single adaptive mutation should spread alone in a hard selective sweep.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from population genetics theory stated in the abstract.

claim: If adaptive mutations occur rarely in the population, then a single adaptive mutation should spread alone in a hard selective sweep.
source: If many adaptive mutations arise simultaneously, then adaptation proceeds by soft selective sweeps in which multiple adaptive mutations spread concomitantly, but if adaptive mutations occur rarely in the population, then a single adaptive mutation should spread alone in a hard selective sweep.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from population genetics theory stated in the abstract.

claim: The study used 6717 HIV-1 consensus sequences from patients treated with first-line therapies between 1989 and 2013.
source: Here, we use 6717 HIV-1 consensus sequences from patients treated with first-line therapies between 1989 and 2013 to confirm that the transition from fast to slow evolution of drug resistance was indeed accompanied with the expected transition from soft to hard selective sweeps.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The transition from fast to slow evolution of drug resistance was accompanied with the expected transition from soft to hard selective sweeps.
source: Here, we use 6717 HIV-1 consensus sequences from patients treated with first-line therapies between 1989 and 2013 to confirm that the transition from fast to slow evolution of drug resistance was indeed accompanied with the expected transition from soft to hard selective sweeps.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study based on analysis of the dataset.

claim: Evolution proceeds via hard sweeps if resistance is unlikely and via soft sweeps if it is likely.
source: This suggests more generally that evolution proceeds via hard sweeps if resistance is unlikely and via soft sweeps if it is likely.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: HIV became a prime example of fast evolutionary change in the first two decades of the HIV epidemic, especially because of the evolution of drug resistance quickly after initiation of treatment.
source: In the first two decades of the HIV epidemic, HIV became a prime example of fast evolutionary change, especially because of the evolution of drug resistance quickly after initiation of treatment.
evidence: This is a historical observation about HIV evolution.

claim: HIV treatments are more clinically effective nowadays and the evolution of drug resistance has become much slower and often does not occur for years if at all.
source: Nowadays, HIV treatments are more clinically effective and the evolution of drug resistance has become much slower and often does not occur for years if at all.
evidence: This is a general observation about modern HIV treatment outcomes.

claim: There are a growing number of examples of fast evolution to selective pressures such as pesticides.
source: Although traditionally evolution was thought to be slow (Darwin, 1859), there are a growing number of examples of fast evolution to selective pressures such as pesticides (Lopes et al., 2008; Daborn et al., 2001; Karasov et al., 2010; Palumbi, 2001), industrialization (Cook et al., 2012), or antibiotics (Laehnemann et al., 2014; Nair et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: There are a growing number of examples of fast evolution to selective pressures such as industrialization.
source: Although traditionally evolution was thought to be slow (Darwin, 1859), there are a growing number of examples of fast evolution to selective pressures such as pesticides (Lopes et al., 2008; Daborn et al., 2001; Karasov et al., 2010; Palumbi, 2001), industrialization (Cook et al., 2012), or antibiotics (Laehnemann et al., 2014; Nair et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: There are a growing number of examples of fast evolution to selective pressures such as antibiotics.
source: Although traditionally evolution was thought to be slow (Darwin, 1859), there are a growing number of examples of fast evolution to selective pressures such as pesticides (Lopes et al., 2008; Daborn et al., 2001; Karasov et al., 2010; Palumbi, 2001), industrialization (Cook et al., 2012), or antibiotics (Laehnemann et al., 2014; Nair et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: HIV's evolutionary speed in treated patients has changed drastically over time.
source: HIV represents an interesting case because its evolutionary speed in treated patients has changed drastically over time.
evidence: This is a general observation about HIV evolution.

claim: Whether populations evolve slowly or quickly is driven by the availability of adaptive mutations.
source: Population genetic theory suggests that whether populations evolve slowly or quickly is driven by the availability of adaptive mutations.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle from population genetics.

claim: In a large population with a high mutation rate, mutations may be available as standing genetic variation or be generated anew every generation, allowing the population to adapt to its environment rapidly.
source: In a large population with a high mutation rate, mutations may be available as standing genetic variation (pre-existing variation) or be generated anew every generation, allowing the population to adapt to its environment rapidly.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle from population genetics.

claim: If adaptive mutations are rare, the population will likely adapt to its environment much more slowly.
source: If adaptive mutations are rare, because the population is small, the mutation rate is low, or only few specific mutations (or combinations of mutations) can help a population adapt, the population will likely adapt to its environment much more slowly.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle from population genetics.

claim: If adaptive mutations are rare (less than one adaptive mutation occurs per generation in the population), the first successful mutation is likely to rise to high frequency before any subsequent adaptive mutations reach appreciable frequencies.
source: If adaptive mutations are rare, i.e., less than one adaptive mutation occurs per generation in the population, the first successful mutation is likely to rise to high frequency before any subsequent adaptive mutations reach appreciable frequencies (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Hard selective sweeps sharply reduce genetic diversity in the population.
source: Hard selective sweeps sharply reduce genetic diversity in the population (Figure 1C) (Smith and Haigh, 1974; Kaplan et al., 1989) in a similar manner to a strong genetic bottleneck.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: When adaptive mutations are common (more than one occurs per generation in the population), the same adaptive mutation may occur several times in a very short time span on different genetic backgrounds.
source: In contrast, when adaptive mutations are common, i.e., more than one occurs per generation in the population, the same adaptive mutation may occur several times in a very short time span on different genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle from population genetics.

claim: Soft selective sweeps are expected to lead to almost no reduction of genetic diversity.
source: This pattern is known as a soft selective sweep and is expected to lead to almost no reduction of genetic diversity (Figure 1F) (Pennings and Hermisson, 2006), comparable to a mild bottleneck.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: The evolution of drug resistance was fast in patients on early anti-retroviral therapies.
source: In HIV, the evolution of drug resistance was fast in patients on early anti-retroviral therapies (Larder et al., 1989), but current multi-drug regimens have substantially slowed the rate of evolution of resistance (Martin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Current multi-drug regimens have substantially slowed the rate of evolution of resistance.
source: In HIV, the evolution of drug resistance was fast in patients on early anti-retroviral therapies (Larder et al., 1989), but current multi-drug regimens have substantially slowed the rate of evolution of resistance (Martin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Population genetic theory predicts that populations should evolve primarily by soft sweeps when resistance is likely and by hard sweeps when resistance is rare.
source: Specifically, population genetic theory predicts that populations should evolve primarily by soft sweeps when resistance is likely and by hard sweeps when resistance is rare.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from population genetics.

claim: Soft sweeps should mark cases of resistance that arise deterministically through many origins while hard sweeps mark cases of rare, 'unlucky' resistance.
source: In essence, soft sweeps should mark cases of resistance that arise deterministically through many origins while hard sweeps mark cases of rare, 'unlucky' resistance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the theoretical predictions.

claim: These predictions have not been tested in HIV or in any natural population.
source: However, these predictions have not been tested in HIV or, in fact, in any natural population.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study.

claim: When hard selective sweeps predominate, there will be a negative correlation between the number of DRMs and genetic diversity in a population.
source: The expectation is that when hard selective sweeps predominate, we will find a negative correlation between the number of DRMs and genetic diversity in a population.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that forms the basis of the study's approach.

claim: When soft selective sweeps predominate, there is no correlation between the number of DRMs and genetic diversity.
source: On the other hand, when soft selective sweeps predominate, we expect to find no such correlation.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that forms the basis of the study's approach.

claim: The study uses 6717 HIV sequences from the same number of patients from the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database.
source: We use 6717 HIV sequences from the same number of patients from the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database (Rhee et al., 2003, https://hivdb.stanford.edu/).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: In standard clinical practice, a sample from a patient's entire HIV population is amplified via PCR and then sequenced using the traditional Sanger method resulting in a single consensus sequence.
source: As such, in standard clinical practice, a sample from a patient's entire HIV population is amplified via PCR and then sequenced using the traditional Sanger method resulting in a single consensus sequence.
evidence: This describes standard clinical sequencing practice.

claim: Genetic diversity may result in ambiguous calls (also referred to as mixtures) in the reported sequence, so that a signal of within-patient genetic diversity is retained even though this sequencing approach generates only a single sequence per patient.
source: Genetic diversity may result in ambiguous calls (also referred to as mixtures) in the reported sequence, so that a signal of within-patient genetic diversity is retained even though this sequencing approach generates only a single sequence per patient.
evidence: This explains how diversity information is retained in consensus sequences.

claim: The study uses ambiguous calls to quantify within-patient genetic diversity, following several other studies.
source: We use the ambiguous calls to quantify within-patient genetic diversity (see Figure 1B, E, grey box), following several other studies (Kouyos et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012; Poon et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the study's methodology, supported by citations to other studies.

claim: It has been shown that the signal from ambiguous calls can be reproduced between laboratories.
source: Although ambiguous calls are an imperfect measure of diversity, it has been shown that the signal from ambiguous calls can be reproduced between laboratories (Shafer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to another study.

claim: Across all sequences, the presence of drug resistance mutations is associated with lower within-patient genetic diversity, marking the occurrence of selective sweeps.
source: We find that, across all sequences, the presence of drug resistance mutations is associated with lower within-patient genetic diversity, marking the occurrence of selective sweeps.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The extent of diversity reduction associated with drug resistance mutations varies with the clinical effectiveness of the treatment.
source: Second, we find that the extent of diversity reduction associated with drug resistance mutations varies with the clinical effectiveness of the treatment - effective drug treatments with low rates of virologic failure (such as NNRTI-based and boosted PI-based regimens) show strong reductions in diversity associated with each additional resistance mutation, a pattern more consistent with hard selective sweeps, whereas treatments that fail more often (such as regimens based only on NRTIs) show no reduction in diversity, a pattern consistent with soft selective sweeps.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Effective drug treatments with low rates of virologic failure (such as NNRTI-based and boosted PI-based regimens) show strong reductions in diversity associated with each additional resistance mutation, a pattern more consistent with hard selective sweeps.
source: Second, we find that the extent of diversity reduction associated with drug resistance mutations varies with the clinical effectiveness of the treatment - effective drug treatments with low rates of virologic failure (such as NNRTI-based and boosted PI-based regimens) show strong reductions in diversity associated with each additional resistance mutation, a pattern more consistent with hard selective sweeps, whereas treatments that fail more often (such as regimens based only on NRTIs) show no reduction in diversity, a pattern consistent with soft selective sweeps.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Treatments that fail more often (such as regimens based only on NRTIs) show no reduction in diversity, a pattern consistent with soft selective sweeps.
source: Second, we find that the extent of diversity reduction associated with drug resistance mutations varies with the clinical effectiveness of the treatment - effective drug treatments with low rates of virologic failure (such as NNRTI-based and boosted PI-based regimens) show strong reductions in diversity associated with each additional resistance mutation, a pattern more consistent with hard selective sweeps, whereas treatments that fail more often (such as regimens based only on NRTIs) show no reduction in diversity, a pattern consistent with soft selective sweeps.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: A lower rate of the production of adaptive mutations should be accompanied by harder sweeps.
source: Although our results do not explain mechanistically how effective treatments lead to harder sweeps of drug resistance mutations, they suggest a more general principle: a lower rate of the production of adaptive mutations should be accompanied by harder sweeps.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the study's findings.

claim: The 6717 patients represent all individuals in the database who were treated with exactly one drug regimen, usually comprising a combination therapy of multiple drugs.
source: The 6717 patients represent all individuals in the database who were treated with exactly one drug regimen, usually comprising a combination therapy of multiple drugs (see Materials and methods: Data collection & filtering).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The patients' viral populations were sequenced after at least some period of treatment, although treatment may or may not have ceased at the time of sequencing and treatment may or may not have failed.
source: The patients' viral populations were sequenced after at least some period of treatment, although treatment may or may not have ceased at the time of sequencing and treatment may or may not have failed.
evidence: This describes the timing of sequencing relative to treatment.

claim: The majority (77%) of patients received a regimen of three drugs.
source: All 6717 patients received some type of therapy (between 1 and 4 drugs), with the majority (77%) receiving a regimen of three drugs.
evidence: This describes the dataset composition.

claim: Nearly all patients received one or two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI), usually paired with a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) or a protease inhibitor (PI), which was boosted with a low dose of ritonavir in some patients.
source: Nearly all patients received one or two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI), usually paired with a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) or a protease inhibitor (PI), which was boosted with a low dose of ritonavir in some patients.
evidence: This describes the treatment regimens in the dataset.

claim: HIV subtypes were varied, with the majority being B (36%), C (34%) or CRF01_AE (13%).
source: HIV subtypes were varied, with the majority being B (36%), C (34%) or CRF01_AE (13%).
evidence: This describes the dataset composition.

claim: None of the remaining subtypes contributed more than 5% of the total sample.
source: None of the remaining subtypes contributed more than 5% of the total sample.
evidence: This describes the dataset composition.

claim: An additional dataset, which we call the clonal dataset, consisted of 11,653 sequences from 740 patients with multiple sequences per patient isolated through clonal amplification and subsequent Sanger sequencing.
source: An additional dataset, which we call the clonal dataset, consisted of 11,653 sequences from 740 patients with multiple sequences per patient isolated through clonal amplification and subsequent Sanger sequencing.
evidence: This describes an additional validation dataset.

claim: The clonal dataset was used for validation purposes only.
source: The clonal dataset was used for validation purposes only.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the clonal dataset.

claim: Clonal within-host nucleotide diversity has a high positive correlation with the percentage of nucleotide calls ambiguous in the D-PCR dataset (r = 0.91, p<2.2 × 10−16).
source: We find that clonal within-host nucleotide diversity has a high positive correlation with the percentage of nucleotide calls ambiguous in the D-PCR dataset (r = 0.91, p<2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a validation result from comparing the two datasets.

claim: A similar pattern holds at the amino acid level (r = 0.85, p<2.2 × 10−16).
source: A similar pattern holds at the amino acid level (r = 0.85, p<2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a validation result from comparing the two datasets.

claim: Ambiguous calls are a reliable proxy for within-patient genetic diversity.
source: We therefore conclude that ambiguous calls are a reliable proxy for within-patient genetic diversity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation analysis.

claim: Among reverse transcriptase and protease DRMs, sequences with the DRM have lower diversity than those with the ancestral state in 14 of 16 cases.
source: Among reverse transcriptase and protease DRMs, sequences with the DRM have lower diversity than those with the ancestral state in 14 of 16 cases, with 7 of the 16 being significantly lower at the 95% confidence level.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 7 of the 16 DRMs show significantly lower diversity at the 95% confidence level.
source: Among reverse transcriptase and protease DRMs, sequences with the DRM have lower diversity than those with the ancestral state in 14 of 16 cases, with 7 of the 16 being significantly lower at the 95% confidence level.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: This reduction in diversity is consistent with expectations after a selective sweep.
source: This reduction in diversity is consistent with expectations after a selective sweep (Smith and Haigh, 1974).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation.

claim: After 4 DRMs, subsequent DRMs do not significantly reduce diversity further.
source: After 4 DRMs, subsequent DRMs do not significantly reduce diversity further.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The observed pattern of DRMs associated with reduced diversity is mainly driven by the patients receiving NNRTI or boosted PI-based treatments.
source: The observed pattern of DRMs associated with reduced diversity is mainly driven by the patients receiving NNRTI or boosted PI-based treatments, as can be seen when separating the above analysis by drug treatment category (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Among patients treated with NRTIs alone or with unboosted PIs, the pattern of DRMs associated with reduced diversity is much less clear.
source: Among patients treated with NRTIs alone or with unboosted PIs, this pattern is much less clear (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The observed pattern holds across the each of the most common subtypes separately.
source: The observed pattern holds across the each of the most common subtypes separately (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: NNRTI-based treatments are preferred to NRTI-based treatments according to general clinical HIV-treatment recommendations.
source: As a categorical approach, we separated regimens based on general clinical HIV-treatment recommendations where NNRTI-based treatments are preferred to NRTI-based treatments, and treatments based on ritonavir-boosted PIs (PI/r) are preferred to treatments based on unboosted PIs.
evidence: This describes clinical treatment recommendations.

claim: Treatments based on ritonavir-boosted PIs (PI/r) are preferred to treatments based on unboosted PIs according to general clinical HIV-treatment recommendations.
source: As a categorical approach, we separated regimens based on general clinical HIV-treatment recommendations where NNRTI-based treatments are preferred to NRTI-based treatments, and treatments based on ritonavir-boosted PIs (PI/r) are preferred to treatments based on unboosted PIs.
evidence: This describes clinical treatment recommendations.

claim: Clinical treatment effectiveness ranged widely, from very low effectiveness (5% of patients virologically suppressed after one year of treatment on AZT monotherapy) to very high effectiveness (100% of patients virologically suppressed after one year of treatment on 3TC+AZT+LPV/r).
source: The two measures (categorical and quantitative) correspond well and clinical treatment effectiveness ranged widely, from very low effectiveness (5% of patients virologically suppressed after one year of treatment on AZT monotherapy) to very high effectiveness (100% of patients virologically suppressed after one year of treatment on 3TC+AZT+LPV/r) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This describes the range of treatment effectiveness in the dataset, shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Even for sequences that carried no resistance mutations, more ambiguous calls were reported over time.
source: We found that even for sequences that carried no resistance mutations, more ambiguous calls were reported over time.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The increase in ambiguous calls over time is likely due to increased awareness of genetic diversity in the HIV community, and not because diversity actually increased.
source: This is likely due to increased awareness of genetic diversity in the HIV community, and not because diversity actually increased.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: Less effective treatments containing only NRTIs were generally associated with a smaller or no reduction in diversity per DRM.
source: Less effective treatments containing only NRTIs were generally associated with a smaller or no reduction in diversity per DRM.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Among sequences from patients receiving highly effective treatments with NNRTIs each fixed DRM is associated with a mean additional 13.6% reduction in diversity as compared to populations with no DRMs (95% confidence interval, 13.0%–14.3%).
source: We find that among sequences from patients receiving highly effective treatments with NNRTIs each fixed DRM is associated with a mean additional 13.6% reduction in diversity as compared to populations with no DRMs (95% confidence interval, 13.0%–14.3%).
evidence: This is a finding from the parametric analysis with statistical support.

claim: Among sequences from patients receiving less effective treatments with only NRTIs, each fixed DRM is associated with a mean additional 4.3% reduction in diversity compared to populations with no DRMs (95% confidence interval, 3.2%–5.3%).
source: Among sequences from patients receiving less effective treatments with only NRTIs, each fixed DRM is associated with a mean additional 4.3% reduction in diversity compared to populations with no DRMs (95% confidence interval, 3.2%–5.3%) (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the parametric analysis with statistical support.

claim: Treatments containing NNRTIs had significantly lower slopes than those treatments containing only NRTIs (p<2.2 × 10−16).
source: We found treatments containing NNRTIs had significantly lower slopes than those treatments containing only NRTIs (p<2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a finding from the parametric analysis with statistical support.

claim: In every one of the 1000 subsampled datasets, the NNRTI category had a more negative slope than the NRTI category.
source: In fact, in every one of the 1000 subsampled datasets, the NNRTI category had a more negative slope than the NRTI category.
evidence: This is a finding from the parametric analysis.

claim: Sequences from effective treatments based on boosted PIs showed a mean additional reduction in diversity of 30.3% with each fixed DRM as compared to populations with no DRMs (95% confidence interval, 19.0%–42.3%).
source: Among PI-based treatments, we found that sequences from effective treatments based on boosted PIs showed a mean additional reduction in diversity of 30.3% with each fixed DRM as compared to populations with no DRMs (95% confidence interval, 19.0%–42.3%).
evidence: This is a finding from the parametric analysis with statistical support.

claim: Sequences from less effective treatments based on unboosted PIs showed a smaller decrease in diversity of 4.3% (95% confidence interval, 2.7%-6.0%) with each fixed DRM.
source: In contrast, sequences from less effective treatments based on unboosted PIs showed a smaller decrease in diversity of 4.3% (95% confidence interval, 2.7%-6.0%) with each fixed DRM (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the parametric analysis with statistical support.

claim: The effect of DRMs on diversity among patients treated with boosted PIs is significantly lower than among patients treated with unboosted PIs (paired Wilcoxon rank-sign test, p<2.2 × 10−16).
source: The effect of DRMs on diversity among patients treated with boosted PIs is significantly lower than among patients treated with unboosted PIs (paired Wilcoxon rank-sign test, p<2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a finding from the parametric analysis with statistical support.

claim: In both treatment classes (RTI-based and PI-based), the fixation of a DRM under more effective treatments leads to a much stronger reduction of diversity than the fixation of a DRM under less effective treatments.
source: In both treatment classes (RTI-based and PI-based), we find that the fixation of a DRM under more effective treatments leads to a much stronger reduction of diversity than the fixation of a DRM under less effective treatments.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the parametric analysis.

claim: A 10% increase in treatment effectiveness is associated with 0.17 fewer ambiguous nucleotide calls with each DRM (95% confidence interval across 1000 fits, [-0.15, -0.19]).
source: We find that a 10% increase in treatment effectiveness is associated with 0.17 fewer ambiguous nucleotide calls with each DRM (95% confidence interval across 1000 fits, [-0.15, -0.19]).
evidence: This is a finding from the non-parametric analysis with statistical support.

claim: Patients given treatments with 50% effectiveness have approximately the same amount of diversity whether they have 0 or 3 DRMs.
source: This means that patients given treatments with 50% effectiveness have approximately the same amount of diversity whether they have 0 or 3 DRMs, but patients on treatments with 80% effectiveness have 54% fewer if they have 3 DRMs as compared to 0.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the non-parametric analysis findings.

claim: Patients on treatments with 80% effectiveness have 54% fewer ambiguous calls if they have 3 DRMs as compared to 0.
source: This means that patients given treatments with 50% effectiveness have approximately the same amount of diversity whether they have 0 or 3 DRMs, but patients on treatments with 80% effectiveness have 54% fewer if they have 3 DRMs as compared to 0.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the non-parametric analysis findings.

claim: This shift from fast to slow evolution of drug resistance has been accompanied by a corresponding shift from soft selective sweeps (in which the same DRM occurs on multiple genetic backgrounds) to hard selective sweeps (in which a DRM occurs only a single time).
source: In this paper, we have shown that this shift from fast to slow evolution of drug resistance has been accompanied by a corresponding shift from soft selective sweeps (in which the same DRM occurs on multiple genetic backgrounds) to hard selective sweeps (in which a DRM occurs only a single time).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Modern treatments have brought HIV into a regime where the viral population must wait until the correct mutation or combination of mutations is generated.
source: This suggests that modern treatments have brought HIV into a regime where the viral population must wait until the correct mutation or combination of mutations is generated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: For any given patient the acquisition of drug resistance has become at least partly an unlucky occurrence, in sharp contrast to the early days of HIV treatment in which all patients predictably failed treatment.
source: This also means that for any given patient the acquisition of drug resistance has become at least partly an unlucky occurrence, in sharp contrast to the early days of HIV treatment in which all patients predictably failed treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Harder sweeps within well-treated patients are also consistent with the overall decrease in the rate of resistance.
source: Harder sweeps within well-treated patients are also consistent with the overall decrease in the rate of resistance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: If the probability of acquiring resistance is low, rare resistance should be generated by hard selective sweeps.
source: However, all these potential mechanisms work to reduce the rate of production of resistant genotypes and the principle is more general: if the probability of acquiring resistance is low, rare resistance should be generated by hard selective sweeps.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the study's findings.
